ABSTRACT 
Continuous wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring is 
difficult to achieve in practice, since arrhythmia classifiers that are accurate 
enough to be clinically useful typically demand more memory and 
computation than an edge device can spare. This project addresses that gap 
through a resource-aware Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework 
built for real-time wearable ECG arrhythmia monitoring. Single-lead ECG 
signals are captured by an AD8232 analog front end wired to an ESP32, 
which streams the sampled data over Wi-Fi to an edge-based processing 
pipeline. There, the signal passes through high-pass, notch and band-pass 
filtering before being segmented into 150-sample beat windows centred on 
each detected R-peak. Every input pairs the normalized ECG waveform 
with two causal RR-context features, yielding a 150 × 3 tensor. Candidate 
architectures are then searched evolutionarily and scored on macro-F1, 
parameter count and inference latency, with pre-pruning enforcing a hard 
120,000-parameter ceiling. The architecture that emerges from this search 
uses just 1,269 trainable parameters and is compressed further through full-
integer INT8 quantization. On 70,396 held-out beats, the quantised model 
reaches 0.8899 accuracy and 0.6188 macro-F1, with an estimated runtime 
memory footprint of only 10,869 bytes. Together, these results point 
toward compact, resource-efficient ECG intelligence for wearable edge 
healthcare.

CHAPTER 1 
INTRODUCTION 
This chapter sets the stage for the rest of the report. It covers the 
background of wearable ECG monitoring, why real-time arrhythmia 
classification is difficult on resource-constrained edge devices, how Neural 
Architecture Search (NAS) helps design compact networks, the motivation 
behind a resource-aware approach, and how the remaining chapters are 
organized. 
Continuous ECG monitoring matters for intelligent healthcare 
precisely because cardiac rhythm abnormalities are often intermittent and 
can easily be missed during a brief clinical visit. Wearable sensing closes 
this gap by letting ECG signals be captured continuously, outside the 
clinic. A compact platform built from a single-lead ECG front end, a 
wireless-enabled microcontroller and a small battery can gather this 
physiological data over long stretches of time [1]. Capturing the signal, 
however, is only half the problem: interpreting the waveform in real time 
calls for computational models that are often too heavy to run on such 
resource-constrained hardware [2]. 
Conventional ECG classifiers tend to be demanding enough to need 
server-class hardware, which pushes wearable systems toward one of two 
compromises: send raw physiological data to a remote platform, or fall 
back to simpler on-device measurements such as heart-rate estimation. The 
first option adds latency, communication overhead and privacy risk; the 
second sacrifices diagnostic depth, since limited local processing caps how 
much information can be extracted directly on the wearable [3]. Both point

1.1 BACKGROUND 
Automated ECG analysis is not a new problem; it has been studied 
for decades. Earlier work generally combined signal-processing techniques 
for QRS detection with classifiers built on morphological and rhythm-
related features. Deep learning changed this by letting one-dimensional 
convolutional networks learn ECG morphology directly from segmented 
signals, cutting down the need for hand-engineered features [4]. Even so, 
many of these high-performing models were not designed with embedded 
deployment constraints in mind [5]. 
Model size and memory usage are tightly constrained on wearable 
and edge platforms [6]. Once application software and communication 
routines have claimed their share of memory, what remains for neural-
network weights can be quite small. Activation memory adds a further 
constraint, since intermediate input and output tensors often need to coexist 
during inference. Embedded microcontrollers can also have limited 
floating-point support, which makes integer-based computation an 
attractive option for resource-constrained deployment [7]. For all these 
reasons, the network architecture cannot be designed in isolation from the 
computational and memory budget available to it. 
The monitoring system built for this project pairs an AD8232-based 
single-lead ECG acquisition stage with an ESP32 microcontroller. The 
ESP32 handles signal acquisition, packetisation, status display and 
wireless transmission, while an edge-side pipeline takes care of signal 
conditioning, beat segmentation and classification. Before beat-level 
analysis begins, the acquired signals are resampled to a common 250 Hz 
rate and passed through high-pass, notch and band-pass filtering stages.

Each detected heartbeat is captured as a fixed 150-sample window 
centred on its R-peak, and the classifier input is built as a 150 × 3 tensor 
combining the normalized ECG waveform with two causal RR-context 
features - a prematurity ratio and an absolute heart-rate-related term. These 
rhythm features are not optional extras: certain arrhythmia types, 
supraventricular ectopic beats in particular, are hard to separate from 
normal beats on morphology alone. 
1.2 NEURAL ARCHITECTURE SEARCH FOR EDGE ECG 
CLASSIFICATION 
Neural Architecture Search automates what used to be a manual 
exercise - choosing the number of convolutional stages, filter counts, 
kernel sizes, strides, pooling operations and dense-layer dimensions - and 
instead treats architecture selection as an optimization problem [8]. Early 
NAS work leaned on reinforcement learning; later methods turned to 
evolutionary and differentiable techniques to bring the search cost down 
[9]. Resource-aware variants go a step further, folding hardware or model-
resource considerations directly into the selection process [10]. 
For this project, the search space is a family of one-dimensional 
convolutional networks, with candidates varying in the number of stages, 
filter count, kernel length, stride, pooling, dropout, activation type and 
dense-head width. An evolutionary strategy - tournament selection, 
mutation and single-point crossover - drives the search, starting from an 
initial population of ten candidates. Before any candidate reaches the 
expensive proxy-training stage, architecture-space pre-pruning discards 
models that exceed the 120,000-parameter constraint. 
The search follows a multi-objective formulation: macro-F1 is 
maximized while parameter count and inference latency are pushed down. 
Macro-F1 is chosen over plain accuracy because the ECG classes are

imbalanced, and macro averaging gives minority classes their fair share of 
weight during selection. Candidates are compared on the Pareto front, with 
weighted objective terms used to break ties among competing 
architectures. 
What the search settled on is a compact design: two convolutional 
stages, global average pooling, a 32-unit dense layer and a five-class 
softmax output. The first convolution uses 16 filters with a kernel length 
of 7 and stride 2; the second uses 8 filters with a kernel length of 3 and 
stride 2. Both convolutional stages use ReLU6 activation with dropout, and 
the resulting architecture holds only 1,269 trainable parameters. 
1.3 MOTIVATION 
These observations set the direction for the project: closing the gap 
between accurate ECG arrhythmia classification and the practical limits of 
wearable edge hardware. The core idea is to let NAS discover, on its own, 
an architecture that fits within a predefined resource budget while still 
classifying usefully. Wearable ECG acquisition, numerical signal

There is also a more general motivation behind this: manually 
designed neural networks have their limits [11]. In the experiments

than the conventional baseline while matching its balanced classification 
performance. That the search chose global average pooling and 
progressively fewer filters across convolutional stages suggests that 
automated search can land on compact configurations a manual design

CHAPTER 2 
LITERATURE REVIEW 
This chapter reviews existing research on neural architecture search, 
lightweight ECG classification, multi-objective optimization, hardware-
aware latency reduction, power-efficient edge inference and model 
quantization. Taken together, the reviewed studies point to a clear need: 
automated architecture design that can balance classification performance 
against the resource limits of wearable and embedded platforms. 
2.1 NEURAL ARCHITECTURE SEARCH 
Neural Architecture Search (NAS) automates the design of neural 
network architectures within a predefined search space. Rather than hand-
picking the number of layers, filters, kernel sizes, strides and other 
architectural components, NAS treats architecture selection as an 
optimization problem - a framing that is especially useful for embedded 
applications, where model accuracy has to be reached under tight memory 
and computational limits. 
Early NAS work showed that automated search could discover 
effective architectures, though at considerable computational cost [12]. 
Later approaches focused on cutting this search cost and tailoring the 
process to specific deployment requirements [8]. ProxylessNAS, for 
instance, was built to search directly for architectures suited to the target 
task and hardware, reducing reliance on expensive proxy tasks [10]. 
For the present ECG application, NAS operates within a constrained 
one-dimensional convolutional search space, with the architecture free to 
vary in the number of stages, filters, kernel length, stride, pooling, dropout, 
dense-layer width and activation function. Restricting the search space this

way keeps unnecessary architectural complexity in check while still letting 
the search explore a range of lightweight CNN configurations. 
2.2 LIGHTWEIGHT DEEP LEARNING FOR ECG 
CLASSIFICATION 
Deep learning has been applied extensively to automatic ECG and 
arrhythmia classification [2]. CNN-based models can learn morphological 
features directly from ECG waveforms, but larger networks are often hard 
to deploy on wearable devices given memory, computation and latency 
limits [3]. 
Lightweight ECG classification research has consequently focused 
on cutting parameter counts while holding on to diagnostic performance 
[13]. Kim et al. built a lightweight CNN for real-time arrhythmia 
classification on a low-power wearable ECG device and showed it running 
on an ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller [14]. Their reported execution time 
and current consumption make the point that model design has to weigh 
computational and electrical cost together, not accuracy in isolation. 
This direction continues in more recent work through compact 
architectures built specifically for resource-constrained ECG systems [15]. 
EdgeECG, for example, proposes an ultra-lightweight network with a 
model compression strategy for real-time arrhythmia classification on low-
power edge devices. Studies like these reinforce the same point: 
architectures need to preserve useful ECG classification performance while 
asking less of the deployment platform. 
2.3 MULTI-OBJECTIVE NEURAL ARCHITECTURE SEARCH 
Traditional architecture optimization tends to treat classification 
accuracy as the main objective. But a highly accurate model can carry a 
large parameter count, demand substantial memory and computation, and 

--- Page 21 ---
9 
introduce inference delay an embedded platform cannot afford. Multi-
objective NAS addresses this by weighing several objectives at once [16]. 
This project uses macro-F1 as the main classification objective, 
alongside minimizing model size and inference latency. Macro-F1 suits the 
ECG dataset well because its class distribution is heavily imbalanced: by 
computing the F1 score separately for each class and then averaging, 
macro-F1 gives every class equal weight, keeping the majority class from 
dominating architecture evaluation. 
Multi-objective NAS also opens the door to several Pareto-efficient 
architectures rather than collapsing everything into a single score [17]. An 
architecture with higher macro-F1 but greater latency can sit on the Pareto 
front alongside another that is smaller and faster but slightly less accurate, 
letting the final choice reflect the requirements of the intended deployment 
platform. 
2.4 LATENCY-AWARE AND HARDWARE-AWARE NAS 
Real-time wearable applications need low inference latency, since 
the model has to keep pace with incoming ECG beats without introducing 
excessive delay. Parameter count and computational complexity are useful 
proxies for efficiency, but they do not always track actual execution time, 
because the same architecture can behave differently across hardware 
platforms [18]. 
MnasNet introduced platform-aware NAS by feeding measured real-
world latency directly into the optimization process, rather than relying 
purely on indirect measures such as FLOPs [19]. Its results showed that 
architectures need to be optimized for the platform they will actually run 
on, since hardware characteristics shape inference speed. ProxylessNAS 

--- Page 22 ---
10 
made a similar case for direct hardware-aware optimization, underlining 
the value of considering the target hardware during NAS [10]. 
This project follows that same principle by factoring inference 
latency into architecture evaluation. The reported latency figures, however, 
come from the host-side development environment rather than the ESP32 
itself, so measuring latency on the target device remains an important next 
step. 
2.5 POWER AND ENERGY-AWARE EDGE COMPUTING 
Power consumption matters for wearable, battery-powered systems, 
since continuous sensing and repeated inference can eat into operating 
lifetime. A smaller model tends to need less computation and memory 
movement, which can translate into lower energy use [11]. Parameter count 
or FLOPs alone, though, are not a reliable stand-in for power consumption, 
because energy use depends heavily on the hardware platform and how the 
model actually executes on it. 
Energy-aware NAS research has begun treating energy as an explicit 
optimization objective in its own right [20]. Several studies note that 
latency is an imperfect proxy for energy, since different neural operations 
carry different energy costs. More recent hardware-aware approaches 
instead build in device-specific energy estimation or direct on-device 
profiling, letting accuracy, latency and energy be optimized together [18]. 
In this project, power is treated as an important deployment concern, 
but it is not directly measured or used as an explicit objective in the 
reported NAS experiment; the current optimization is limited to macro-F1, 
parameter count and inference latency. Measuring ESP32 power directly 
and building explicit power-aware NAS are left as future extensions.

2.6 QUANTIZATION AND RESOURCE-EFFICIENT 
DEPLOYMENT 
Quantization is a key technique for cutting the resource requirements 
of neural networks bound for embedded deployment [7]. Full-integer INT8 
quantization converts floating-point weights and activations into eight-bit 
integer form, shrinking memory requirements and making integer-based 
inference a better fit for microcontroller-class platforms [20]. 
Here, post-training INT8 quantization is applied after the NAS 
architecture has been selected and fully trained, on a network with 1,269 
trainable parameters. Doing so drops the estimated runtime memory from 
43,476 bytes (FP32) to 10,869 bytes (INT8) - roughly a fourfold reduction 
- while the serialized model size falls from 9.5 kB to 8.23 kB. 
The literature also makes clear that architecture optimization and 
embedded deployment need to be considered together. Lightweight ECG 
models have been successfully moved onto microcontroller platforms [14], 
and hardware-aware NAS frameworks stress evaluating architectures 
against the characteristics of the actual target device [17]. In this project, 
the immediate deployment step is moving the quantised model from the 
host or edge server onto the ESP32 using an embedded inference runtime 
such as TensorFlow Lite Micro [6]. 
2.7 SUMMARY OF LITERATURE REVIEW 
Overall, the literature makes it clear that neural architecture design 
for wearable ECG systems cannot rest on classification accuracy alone. 
Lightweight CNN research underlines the importance of smaller models 
[13], hardware-aware NAS shows that actual latency is tied to the 
deployment platform [19], and energy-aware studies argue that power

should be optimized as its own objective rather than inferred from 
parameter count or FLOPs [20]. 
The reviewed work therefore motivates a resource-aware, multi-
objective NAS framework for the proposed ECG system. Here, macro-F1, 
parameter count and inference latency are folded into the search, with a 
120,000-parameter pre-pruning constraint and Pareto-based selection used 
to filter out unsuitable architectures before expensive evaluation. The 
selected architecture ends up with only 1,269 parameters and reaches 
0.8899 accuracy and 0.6188 macro-F1 after INT8 quantization, while 
cutting estimated runtime memory substantially relative to the FP32 model. 
One gap that remains is the lack of direct target-device latency and 
power measurements in the current implementation. The next chapter turns

analysis, quantization and deployment strategy in detail.

CHAPTER 3 
PROBLEM IDENTIFICATION 
This chapter pins down the problem the project addresses: deploying 
neural networks for wearable ECG arrhythmia classification. It focuses on 
where conventional, manually designed models fall short, and makes the 
case for multi-objective neural architecture search that balances 
classification performance against model size, inference latency and, 
eventually, power. 
3.1 PROBLEM STATEMENT 
Wearable ECG monitoring needs continuous signal analysis under 
the tight computational and memory budget of embedded and edge 
devices. A network optimized purely for classification accuracy can end 
up with excessive parameters, heavier memory and computation demands, 
and higher inference cost - all of which make direct deployment on a 
resource-constrained platform difficult [21]. 
This problem is sharper still for arrhythmia classification because 
the ECG dataset is highly imbalanced [22]. Optimizing for overall 
accuracy alone lets the majority Normal class dominate evaluation, leaving 
minority classes such as Fusion under-represented. A sound architecture-
selection process therefore needs a balanced classification measure like 
macro-F1, alongside deployment-related resource requirements. 
Inference latency is a further constraint for real-time ECG 
monitoring, since predictions need to be produced promptly as beats are 
processed. Running on a battery-powered wearable node also makes 
computational and energy efficiency important design considerations. That 
said, the present implementation does not directly measure or optimize 

--- Page 26 ---
14 
classifier power consumption, and the reported latency comes from the 
host-side development environment rather than the ESP32 itself. 
The problem this work sets out to solve, then, is building an 
automated architecture-selection mechanism that can find compact ECG 
classification networks while keeping predictive performance balanced 
and deployment cost low. The proposed approach tackles this through 
multi-objective NAS using macro-F1, parameter count and inference

7.4 MULTI-OBJECTIVE EVALUATION 
Each surviving architecture is judged on its classification 
performance and deployment-related resource requirements. Macro-F1, 
rather than raw accuracy, is the principal classification metric here, since 
the ECG dataset has a highly imbalanced distribution of heartbeat classes 
and macro-F1 gives a more balanced picture of performance across all of 
them. 
For each heartbeat class, precision and recall combine into a class-
level F1 score, and these scores are then averaged across all classes to get 
macro-F1. This gives every class equal weight during architecture 
evaluation and stops the majority Normal class from single-handedly 
determining how good an architecture looks. 
Parameter count is the second evaluation objective. Fewer 
parameters mean less storage for the trained model and, often, lower 
memory and computational demand at deployment - a point that matters 
particularly for wearable ECG systems, where memory and processing 
resources are limited. 
Inference latency is the third objective, capturing how long the 
architecture takes to process an ECG input and produce a classification 
result. Real-time wearable monitoring needs classification results with 
minimal delay, so lower-latency architectures are preferred from a 
deployment standpoint. 
All three objectives are considered together during evaluation: 
macro-F1 is maximized to keep classification performance balanced across 
heartbeat classes, while parameter count and inference latency are both 
minimized to reduce model size, memory requirements, and improve 
responsiveness during real-time operation.

Macro-F1, parameter count and inference latency values are used 
together when comparing architectures, so the multi-objective evaluation 
weighs classification quality and deployment efficiency together rather 
than leaning on accuracy alone. 
7.5 PARETO ANALYSIS AND WEIGHTED FITNESS 
Because these objectives can conflict, the search may turn up 
architectures with quite different performance-resource profiles - one 
might reach higher macro-F1 at the cost of more parameters and greater 
latency, while another trades a little classification performance for being 
smaller and faster. 
Pareto analysis is used here to identify non-dominated architectures: 
a candidate is dominated when another architecture matches or beats it on 
every objective and strictly beats it on at least one, and the architectures 
that are not dominated by anything form the Pareto front. 
This Pareto stage keeps architectures with different trade-offs in 
play, rather than forcing the search to commit to a single solution too early. 
After Pareto analysis, a weighted fitness measure guides selection toward 
the preferred balance between classification performance and resource 
efficiency. 
The reported methodology considers two weighting configurations: 
an edge-balanced configuration that gives resource efficiency more relative 
weight, and an accuracy-first configuration that leans more toward 
predictive performance. Together they show how the preferred final 
architecture can shift depending on deployment requirements. 
This weighted evaluation acts as a decision mechanism once the 
candidate architectures have already been scored against their individual 
objectives.

Abstract— Connected vehicles require low latency and 
secure communication links to be incorporated. But quantum 
computers with Shor algorithm can break the vehicular 
networks and the large security algorithms already in use, i.e., 
RSA, ECC and ECDSA. This article describes a quantum first-
mover platooning communication in vehicles. We described our 
security framework using two of the four National Institute of 
Standards and Technologies (NIST) approved algorithms, 
CRYSTALS-Kyber (key encapsulation) and CRYSTALS-
Dilithium (digital signatures). To keep the overhead of per-
message overhead low in order to provide real-time platooning, 
we applied AES-256-GCM to stream all of the post-handshake 
traffic. The system set the following benchmarks: <4 millisecond 
(ms) key exchange, 1.13 ms average round trip time (RTT) and 
35 ms latency (minimal and under the 100 ms platooning 
ceiling). As of now, the system can support 200 messages per 
second, key exchange success rate of 99.9 and a fail safe cutover 
of 200 ms. The main value of this research is to demonstrate the 
fact that compliance to quantum security does not affect the 
real-time operation in any aspect.

I. INTRODUCTION 
The modern intelligent transport systems harness the real-
time V2V communication systems to coordinate vehicles in 
manners not possible with human drivers, such as formation 
shooting, cooperative braking, and collision warnings. 
Algorithms to secure such a communication link are an 
engineering marvel, but that they are being developed in a 
world with quantum computers, and to not-factorable-to-
polynomial-time problems in the classical world is wanting. 
The problems are the most acute in case of vehicle 
platooning. The leader car sends its speed and position, and 
the followers adapt their speed accordingly. In this case, the 
milliseconds latency can be the difference between an 
accident and safe driving. An attacker who spoof(s) (or even 
temporarily) cause a collision (or pile-up) situation. Our RSA 
and ECC-based cryptography (which have no survival against 
Shor’s algorithm) is the cryptographic glue of 'what is to be''. 
As a solution to the problem, we are on the building-blocks 
of Shor’s algorithm. The quantum world will eventually have 
a more efficient and powerful algorithm compared with any 
other system (even the poly time classical domain) that has a 
time scale of less than a milliseconds (or even less than a 
second). The future of a possible solution to the problem is the 
post-quantum cryptographies which have the honour of the 
NIST validation. 
Here in this paper, we present a proven working vehicle-
to-vehicle (V2V) platooning system, for the first time, 
covering the design rationale, cryptographic handshake, fail-
safe and the balanced results of our latency and quantum 
cryptographic proof results. Our intention is not to produce a 
verifiable proof of but to produce a demonstrable fact that the 
quantum cryptography may yet be proof against the problem 
of collision avoidance or platooning yet have no more of a 
time-constraint than that of sub-100 milliseconds. 
II. LITERATURE SURVEY 
A. Classical Security in Vehicular Networks 
The trust model of vehicular communication systems 
based on the 802.11p standard and DSRC is identical to that 
of PKI-based systems; i.e. each vehicle is issued with a 
certificate by a trusted third party and the signatures on the 
outgoing messages are built using the respective private keys 
[4]. It cannot be scaled as the cost of CRL validation is higher, 
the cost of verifying the signatures on the outgoing messages 
is high since they have to verify simultaneously and the high 
mobility of the vehicles is a violation of the assumption that 
the state information in the certificates is always constant. 
Even more basic is the fact that RSA and ECC have been 
shown to be broken by the algorithm of Shor, and so such 
systems are on a time-bomb. 
Nevertheless, despite its popularity, the PKI-based 
architecture has three architectural limitations in deploying the 
solution to car scenario. To begin with, the overheads involved 
in CRL validation have a scaling of the density of cars in a 
convoy, meaning so that in an example of a 100 vehicle 
convoy with cars transmitting to each other at 50 Htz, all of 
the nodes must continuously perform and propagate CRL 
validations, and therefore use a significant fraction of the total 
bandwidth allocated to the DSRC communications. Second, 
signature verification using ECC schemes can have higher 
latencies than 10-50 ms per validation because of multiple 
messages in a traffic environment [6] - something which is 
unacceptable with hard and fast deadlines of sub100 ms 
platooning uses. Lastly, and probably most crucially, ECC and 
RSA algorithms utilize the intractability of integer 
factorization and discrete logarithms, whose solutions can be 
found by Shor algorithm in a large-enough quantum processor 
in a time factorial time [15].

B. Post-Quantum Cryptography Advances 
NIST conducted the standardization process in 2024 and 
discovered Kyber and Dilithium to be the key encapsulation 
and signature primary algorithms respectively [2], [3]. Kyber 
is built on the Module LWE, Dilithium is built on the Module 
LWE and Short Integer Solutions. The latter is implemented 
in a library that is hardware-optimized and is efficient on 
commodity hardware [5], [6]. Hybrid ECC-Kyber protocols 
are compatible backwards, but twice as expensive to 
handshake, not a good bargain when designing a clean-sheet 
vehicle. 
C. Lattice-Based Cryptography in Vehicular Network 
Security 
Numerous publications, which examine the underlying 
specific implementation of the PQC algorithms with respect 
to vehicles and transportations on lattices, have also appeared 
recently. To illustrate this concept, Li et al. [7] outlined lattice 
cryptography within their article and provided a detailed 
analysis of the system of autonomous vehicles through the 
prism of NTRU, MLWE and MSIS families of algorithms and 
their implementation in: V2V authentication; OTA firmware 
update; and edge-assisted data aggregation. The analysis of 
FPGA acceleration shows that Kyber with optimization can 
produce keys using software with less than 1.5 ms (less than 
0.1 ms respectively) which obviously opens the prospects of 
the automotive application. In a comparative study of multiple 
PQC algorithm versions (ARM Cortex-A72 automotive 
processors used) (Kandappu et al, 2020), Dilithium3 signature 
verification requires less than 2.5 ms - and that too much 
shorter than 20 ms inter-beacon time period (at 50 Hz). Kyber-
768 has turned out to be the most effective candidate. 
D. Platooning Security and Real-Time Communication 
Constraints 
Platooning comes with its own set of strict constraints 
regarding the performance of the security systems of vehicles. 
The platooned vehicles running at headway distances of 5-6 
meters on highways need control loop updates of 10-50 Hz 
with an end-to-end delay of less than 100 ms; security 
overheads exceeding this threshold will have disastrous 
consequences for the platoon's safety. According to Zhang et 
al. [8], Dilithium3 verification can be implemented in NS-3 
simulations for 10 Hz beaconing when processing occurs 
locally to the communication system. However, no actual 
testbed was used in this study, and there was no measurement 
of the key exchange delays, end-to-end command 
transmission, and fail-safeness during communication 
interruption. 
E. Research Gap 
A literature review shows that there are three significant 
gaps that are addressed by the present work. To begin with, 
none of the published studies has utilized both CRYSTALS-
Kyber and CRYSTALS-Dilithium in a live wireless testbed 
V2V at the same time, end to end roundtrip latency in the live 
wireless environment, and lifecycle of session-keys, since join 
via indefinite operation, and fail-safe exit. PQC algorithms are 
either evaluated outside of a control loop around a vehicle 
[3][12] or on a testbed using wires [10] or by simulation 
against one on a hardware prototype [8]. Second, there is no 
prior literature to find the fail safe response time of a platoon 
with a PQC secured communications under the impact of 
communications disruption which can be directly applied to 
the automotive safety standards. Third, previous studies have 
discovered that in this scenario, the impossibility to use PQC 
and platooning concurring is dependent on the length of the 
per-message latency of PQC computation, and that session-
key architecture type, in this scenario, need not be 
indicatively, and that the costly lattice operations involved in 
PQC computation are restricted to the join stage. All three 
gaps have been bridged in the current system using a prototype 
of PQC-native on live 802.11 equipment.

C. Security Protocol Design 
In the beginning of every session, a unique Kyber key pair 
is generated, as well as a unique Dilithium pair for every 
vehicle. When the follower establishes a connection with the 
leader, the follower sends its Kyber public key. The leader 
then sends a message, which includes the randomly generated 
shared secret. The message is encapsulated with the follower's 
public key. The follower is then able to decapsulate the 
message and retrieve the secret. The shared secret is never sent 
in plaintext, though. An attacker will only be able to see the 
encapsulated message, which is difficult to break. 
 
The shared secret is then used to derive the AES-256-
GCM session key. Before the handshake is completed, the 
leader signs the challenge with the use of Dilithium. This must 
then be verified by the follower. This is all done in such a way 
that the leader as well as the follower are legit. This is then 
followed by communication with the use of AES-GCM. There 
is no use of PQC on the messages, which keeps the 
communication extremely fast. 
D. Platoon Coordination 
The CACC controller computes the safe distance with the 
lead vehicle by using the equation d = d_min + t_hw * 
v_current. In the equation above, d_min is the minimum 
distance threshold value, which can be adjusted according to 
the type of vehicle. The data sent through the UDP packets 
includes the speed, position, rate of change, sequence number, 
and the time stamp. The receiver side will drop the packets 
with time stamp not within 500 ms. The packets are also 
dropped to avoid the replay attack if the sequence number is 
not monotonically increasing. 
E. Fail Safe Mechanism 
In the absence of an authentic packet within the time-out 
period, the vehicle returns to standalone cruise control within 
200 ms by increasing the gap with the preceding vehicle to a 
safe distance. Re-entry is possible only with a new authentic 
beacon from the leader.

D. Comparison with Existing Approaches 
PKI-based systems with ECC have an operational time of 
10 ms to 50 ms for each round trip with realistic traffic loads. 
Our RTT of 1.13 ms is one order of magnitude faster due to 
the PQC cost being entirely incurred in the setup. Hybrid 
approaches using both ECC and Kyber are slower than each 
individual solution due to the PQC ciphertext overhead and 
the ECC computation time. A PQC-native solution does not 
have the disadvantage of double work. 
V. CONCLUSION 
However, building a quantum-resistant V2V system with 
real-time capabilities is more an engineering problem than a 
cryptographic problem. The cryptographic solutions have 
been developed and standardized by NIST. The problem is 
whether we can fit within the latency constraints that safety-
critical applications require. Our prototype demonstrates this 
with actual measurements: CRYSTALS-Kyber and Dilithium 
have session establishment within 4 ms, AES-GCM is under 
0.11 ms for per-message overhead, and we achieve an end-to-
end latency of 35 ms at 200 msg/sec with 99.9% key exchange 
reliability. 
Performance under dedicated hardware for V2X radios, in 
dense multi-vehicle scenes, and under adversary channel 
conditions remains to be tested. These would be the next steps, 
along with acceleration for embedded systems using 
FPGAs/ASICS and machine learning-based solutions for 
application-layer anomalies without direct impact on 
cryptographic primitives.

ABSTRACT 
The rapid advancement of autonomous and connected vehicles has 
revolutionized modern transportation, enabling applications such as 
platooning, collision avoidance, and cooperative adaptive cruise control 
(CACC). However, traditional Public Key Infrastructure (PKI)-based security 
frameworks, which rely on RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), are 
increasingly vulnerable to quantum computing threats. Quantum algorithms 
like Shor’s algorithm can break these classical cryptographic methods, posing 
a significant risk to the long-term security of vehicular networks. This paper 
presents a quantum-resistant V2V platooning communication system that 
integrates post-quantum cryptographic algorithms (CRYSTALS-Kyber and 
CRYSTALS-Dilithium) with real-time communication protocols to ensure 
confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity in vehicular networks.The proposed 
system achieves low-latency communication with an end-to-end latency of 35 
ms, well within the 100 ms threshold required for real-time platooning 
applications. It also incorporates fail-safe mechanisms that allow vehicles to 
exit platoon mode safely within 200 ms in the event of communication 
failures, ensuring vehicle safety and traffic flow stability. The modular 
architecture of the system supports scalability, maintainability, and future 
upgrades, making it adaptable to evolving security and technological 
requirements.Experimental results demonstrate the system’s efficiency and 
reliability, with 99.9% success in key exchange, <10 ms message 
authentication time, and 200 messages per second throughput. Despite these 
strengths, challenges such as computational overhead, network latency, and 
integration with existing infrastructure remain.

INTRODUCTION 
The rapid advancement of Intelligent Transportation Systems 
 has 
revolutionized modern vehicular technology by enabling seamless communication 
between vehicles, infrastructure, and surrounding environments. Among these 
advancements, Vehicle-to-Vehicle communication has emerged as a fundamental 
technology that enables vehicles to exchange real-time information such as speed, 
position, acceleration, braking status, and road conditions. This communication plays 
a critical role in enhancing road safety, reducing traffic congestion, and enabling 
autonomous driving systems. 
One of the most important applications of V2V communication is vehicle 
platooning, where multiple vehicles travel in a coordinated formation with minimal 
inter-vehicle distance. In such systems, a lead vehicle controls the movement, while 
follower vehicles adjust their speed and position based on real-time data received from 
the leader and neighboring vehicles. This coordinated movement improves fuel 
efficiency, optimizes road usage, and enhances driving comfort. However, the 
effectiveness of platooning depends heavily on the reliability, accuracy, and security 
of the communication system. 
Despite the advancements in V2V communication, current systems primarily 
rely on classical cryptographic techniques such as RSA and Elliptic Curve 
Cryptography to ensure secure communication. These cryptographic algorithms are 
widely used for authentication, key exchange, and data encryption. While they provide 
strong security under classical computational models, they are fundamentally 
vulnerable to attacks from quantum computers. 
Quantum computing introduces a paradigm shift in computational capabilities 
by leveraging quantum mechanical phenomena such as superposition and 
entanglement. Quantum algorithms, particularly Shor’s Algorithm[1], can efficiently 
solve problems such as integer factorization and discrete logarithms, which form the

successful attack on the communication system could lead to false data injection, 
vehicle impersonation, or message tampering, potentially resulting in catastrophic 
consequences such as accidents and traffic disruptions. 
To address these challenges, Post-Quantum Cryptography has been proposed as 
a new generation of cryptographic algorithms that are resistant to both classical and 
quantum attacks. PQC algorithms are based on mathematically hard problems such as

via a wireless network. Each node simulates a vehicle and performs communication,

the practical feasibility of integrating PQC into V2V communication systems

The transition toward connected and autonomous transportation systems has 
fundamentally reshaped the role of inter-vehicle communication. Vehicle-to-Vehicle 
(V2V) communication enables distributed coordination among vehicles by facilitating 
the continuous exchange of safety-critical state information, including velocity, 
acceleration, heading, and relative positioning. Such capabilities are particularly 
central to platooning systems, where vehicles operate in tightly coupled formations to 
enhance traffic throughput, reduce fuel consumption, and improve road safety. 
However, the effectiveness of these systems is inherently dependent on the integrity, 
authenticity, and timeliness of the exchanged information. 
Existing vehicular communication frameworks have largely been developed 
within the paradigm of Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks (VANETs), leveraging standards 
such as IEEE 802.11p and Dedicated Short-Range Communications. These 
frameworks incorporate Public Key Infrastructure models to establish trust among 
vehicles, with security services implemented using classical cryptographic primitives 
such as RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography . While these mechanisms provide 
adequate protection in contemporary computing environments, their long-term 
viability is fundamentally challenged by the emergence of quantum computing. 
Quantum computing introduces a disruptive threat model in which widely 
deployed cryptographic schemes become computationally insecure. In particular, 
Shor’s algorithm enables efficient factorization of large integers and computation of 
discrete logarithms, effectively breaking RSA and ECC-based systems [1]. Given that 
vehicular communication systems are expected to operate over extended lifecycles, 
the inability of classical cryptography to withstand quantum adversaries represents a 
critical limitation. 
To address this vulnerability, Post-Quantum Cryptography  has been proposed

problems that are conjectured to remain intractable even for quantum computers. 
Among these, lattice-based cryptography has emerged as the most promising

and suitability for constrained environments. 
The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has identified 
CRYSTALS-Kyber and CRYSTALS-Dilithium as leading algorithms for post-

its handshake procedures, retransmission strategies, and congestion control introduce 
non-deterministic delays. Consequently, User Datagram Protocol  is widely adopted in 
vehicular systems due to its connectionless design, minimal overhead, and 
deterministic latency characteristics [4]. Although UDP does not inherently provide 
reliability or security, these features can be implemented at the application layer in a 
manner tailored to vehicular requirements.

2.1 CLASSICAL SECURITY APPROACHES IN VEHICULAR NETWORKS 
Classical security approaches in vehicular networks are primarily based on 
Public Key Infrastructure, which provides a structured framework for establishing 
trust among communicating entities. In this model, each vehicle is assigned a digital 
certificate issued by a trusted Certificate Authority , enabling it to authenticate itself 
and verify the identity of other vehicles in the network. Cryptographic operations 
within this framework are typically implemented using well-established algorithms 
such as RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography . These techniques offer essential 
security services, including authentication through digital signatures, confidentiality 
through encryption, and data integrity verification. 
Among these, ECC is often preferred in vehicular systems due to its efficiency, 
as it provides comparable security to RSA with smaller key sizes and reduced 
computational overhead. In practice, vehicles sign outgoing messages using their 
private keys and attach certificates, allowing receiving vehicles to verify the 
authenticity and integrity of the transmitted data. This mechanism is particularly 
important in safety-critical applications such as collision avoidance and platoon 
coordination, where decisions are made based on real-time information exchanged 
between vehicles. 
Despite these advantages, PKI-based systems introduce several practical 
challenges when applied to vehicular networks. One of the primary concerns is the 
overhead associated with certificate management. Vehicles must continuously validate 
certificates, check their validity, and ensure they have not been revoked. This process 
often involves accessing Certificate Revocation Lists, which must be frequently 
updated and distributed. In large-scale and highly dynamic environments, maintaining 
and disseminating this information efficiently becomes increasingly difficult, affecting 
system scalability.

Latency is another critical factor. Vehicular communication requires near-
instantaneous processing of incoming messages, especially in time-sensitive scenarios. 
However, the verification of digital signatures and certificates introduces 
computational delays. In dense traffic conditions, where vehicles receive multiple 
messages simultaneously, this overhead can accumulate and impact real-time 
responsiveness. 
The dynamic nature of vehicular networks further complicates security 
implementation. Vehicles frequently encounter new communication partners as they 
move, requiring rapid authentication without relying on stable connections. This 
transient behavior challenges traditional PKI mechanisms, which were originally 
designed for more stable network environments. 
Privacy considerations also play a significant role. To prevent tracking, vehicles 
often use pseudonymous certificates that change periodically. While this enhances 
privacy, it increases the complexity of certificate management and adds additional 
processing and communication overhead. 
A more fundamental limitation of classical approaches lies in their vulnerability 
to emerging quantum computing threats. Algorithms such as RSA and ECC rely on 
mathematical problems that can be efficiently solved using quantum algorithms like 
Shor’s algorithm. This raises concerns about the long-term security of vehicular 
communication systems, particularly given their extended operational lifetimes. 
In summary, classical PKI-based security mechanisms have provided a reliable 
foundation for early vehicular communication systems. However, their limitations in 
terms of scalability, latency, privacy management, and quantum vulnerability highlight 
the need for more advanced and future-proof security solutions.Researchers and 
industry stakeholders are increasingly focusing on developing and standardizing 
quantum-resistant algorithms to address these challenges.

applications. Furthermore, many existing solutions treat security as a separate layer 
rather than integrating it seamlessly into the communication architecture, leading to 
inefficiencies in latency-sensitive scenarios such as vehicle platooning. There is also a 
noticeable lack of practical implementations that demonstrate a balanced combination 
of strong security, low latency, and scalability in highly dynamic vehicular 
environments.

communication framework that can ensure robust security against both current and 
future threats while maintaining the performance requirements of real-time 
applications. Specifically, there is a need for a system that can provide quantum-

operate efficiently in decentralized and high-mobility conditions. Addressing this 
problem requires moving beyond conventional and hybrid approaches toward a fully 
integrated architecture that combines post-quantum cryptographic techniques with 
lightweight communication protocols. The proposed work aims to fill this gap by 
developing a secure, low-latency, and scalable V2V communication system tailored 
for modern and future vehicular networks.The proposed system aims to bridge this 
gap by integrating quantum-resistant cryptography with low-latency communication

SYSTEM DESIGN 
The proposed system implements a quantum-resistant Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) 
communication framework designed specifically for real-time platooning applications. 
The architecture operates within a simulated VANET environment, where vehicles 
communicate dynamically over a wireless network. To ensure both security and 
performance, the system adopts a hybrid cryptographic approach that combines post-
quantum cryptography with efficient symmetric encryption. 
At the initial stage of communication, each vehicle node generates its own 
public–private key pairs using CRYSTALS-Kyber(10) for key exchange and 
CRYSTALS-Dilithium for authentication. When a communication session is initiated, 
the sender performs a one-time secure key exchange using the receiver’s Kyber public 
key. Through the encapsulation and decapsulation process, both communicating 
vehicles derive a shared session key without directly transmitting it over the network. 
This mechanism ensures resistance against both classical and quantum cryptographic 
attacks. 
Following key establishment, an initial authentication phase is executed using 
Dilithium digital signatures. During this step, the sender signs a verification message, 
and the receiver validates the signature using the sender’s public key. This confirms 
the identity of the communicating node and prevents unauthorized vehicle 
participation. To optimize real-time performance, this authentication process is 
performed only once during session establishment, thereby reducing computational 
overhead associated with repeated post-quantum operations. 
Once the secure session is established, the system transitions to symmetric 
cryptographic operations for continuous communication. All subsequent V2V 
messages are encrypted using AES-GCM with the shared session key.

Kyber Key Encapsulation: The follower vehicle uses the leader’s Kyber public 
key to encapsulate a shared secret.

Key Decapsulation: The leader uses its Kyber private key to decapsulate the 
shared secret. 
3.
Session Key Establishment: Both vehicles now share a symmetric session key 
for AES-GCM encryption.

4.3 Cryptographic Implementation: Ensuring Quantum Resistance 
Security forms the core foundation of the proposed system, as vehicular 
communication involves the exchange of safety-critical information that must remain 
protected from both current and future threats. To achieve this, the system integrates 
post-quantum cryptographic mechanisms using the LibOQS (Open Quantum Safe) 
library, which provides reliable and optimized implementations of quantum-resistant 
algorithms. 
The key exchange process is implemented using CRYSTALS-Kyber, a lattice-
based post-quantum algorithm selected by NIST for its strong security and efficiency. 
Kyber enables two communicating vehicles to securely establish a shared session key 
through encapsulation and decapsulation without directly transmitting the key over the 
network. This ensures that even if an attacker intercepts the communication, the key 
cannot be derived, making the system resistant to both classical and quantum attacks. 
For authentication, the system uses CRYSTALS-Dilithium, a post-quantum 
digital signature scheme. During the initial communication phase, messages are signed 
using Dilithium to verify the identity of the sender and ensure that the data has not 
been altered. This prevents attacks such as impersonation and message tampering, 
which are critical threats in vehicular environments. To maintain efficiency, this 
authentication process is performed primarily during session establishment, reducing 
the computational overhead during continuous communication. 
Once a secure session is established, the system transitions to AES-GCM 
(Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode) for encrypting all 
subsequent messages. AES-GCM is chosen for its high performance and ability to 
provide both confidentiality and integrity through authenticated encryption. It ensures 
that transmitted data remains private while also detecting any unauthorized 
modifications through authentication tags.
